fields.definition: The lead technician who supervises a work crew or department during a live event's load-in, setup, show operation, and load-out, coordinating the crew's tasks, schedule, and safety while serving as the department's point of contact for the production manager and stage manager.
fields.plain_english: A crew chief is the boss of a small work team on a show. They plan what each person does, keep everyone on schedule, and make sure the work is done safely.
fields.purpose_function: The role gives each department a single accountable leader who directs the crew's work, keeps the schedule and safety plan on track, and provides a clear line of communication up to production management.
fields.practical_application: On a show day the crew chief assigns tasks at load-in, oversees rigging, staging, or audio setup, calls breaks, tracks progress against the schedule, and reports readiness to the production or stage manager.
common_mistakes: Assuming the crew chief personally does all the technical work rather than directing and coordinating the crew.
Confusing the crew chief with the production manager; the crew chief leads one crew or department, while the production manager oversees the whole production.
UNSAFE: Treating the crew chief's safety oversight as optional and skipping crew briefings on rigging, fall protection, and manual handling before load-in.
scenario_contexts: Leading a local stagehand crew through a festival stage load-in and changeover.
Directing the audio department's setup and reporting readiness to the production manager.
Overseeing a load-out so gear is safely struck, cased, and loaded on schedule.

fields.definition: A visiting mix engineer who travels with a performing act, or is brought in for a specific event, and mixes on the venue's provided sound system rather than being employed by the venue; also called a visiting or touring engineer.
fields.plain_english: A guest engineer is a sound mixer who comes in with the band instead of working for the venue. They mix the show on the venue gear that they did not set up.
fields.purpose_function: The role lets a touring act keep a consistent mix and a trusted engineer who knows the show, while still using whatever installed or supplied sound system each venue provides.
fields.practical_application: A guest engineer arrives at load-in, meets the house engineer, learns the venue's system, patch, and limits, then mixes front-of-house or monitors for their act through soundcheck and the show.
common_mistakes: Confusing the guest engineer with the house engineer; the guest travels with the act while the house engineer works for the venue.
Assuming the guest engineer is responsible for setting up or maintaining the venue system, which is the house engineer's or systems engineer's job.
UNSAFE: Driving an unfamiliar house PA past its rated limits or safe SPL exposure levels without checking the system's headroom, limiter settings, and the operator's own hearing protection.
scenario_contexts: A touring band's engineer mixing front-of-house on a club's installed system.
Meeting the house engineer at load-in to review the patch and system limits.
Taking over the mix from the house engineer after the opening act's set.

fields.definition: The audio engineer employed by or resident at a venue who operates and maintains the venue's installed sound system, mixes acts that arrive without their own engineer, and provides technical support and orientation to visiting guest engineers.
fields.plain_english: A house engineer works for the venue, not the band. They know the venue sound system, mix acts that have no engineer, and help visiting engineers use the gear.
fields.purpose_function: The role gives the venue an in-house expert who keeps the sound system working, ensures a reliable mix for every act, and helps touring engineers get up to speed quickly on the local rig.
fields.practical_application: A house engineer sets up and line-checks the venue PA, mixes opening or unrepresented acts, and walks guest engineers through the console, patch, and system limits at load-in.
common_mistakes: Confusing the house engineer with a touring or guest engineer; the house engineer is tied to the venue and its installed system.
Assuming the house engineer only mixes, when they also maintain, troubleshoot, and often manage the venue's audio inventory.
UNSAFE: Defeating protective measures such as system limiters or the correct power-up and power-down order to gain more level, risking driver damage and unsafe SPL for audience and crew.
scenario_contexts: Mixing a local opening act that arrived without its own engineer.
Orienting a touring guest engineer to the venue's console and patch at load-in.
Troubleshooting a dead channel in the installed PA before doors.

fields.definition: A technician assigned to the stage who sets up, maintains, and operates onstage equipment during a live event — running and patching microphone and instrument lines, positioning mics, monitors, and backline, managing stage cabling, and assisting performers and the monitor engineer through setup, changeovers, and the performance.
fields.plain_english: A stage tech is the crew member who works up on the stage. They set up mics, monitors, and cables, and help the band and the monitor mixer during the show.
fields.purpose_function: The role keeps the stage set up correctly and running smoothly so performers have working mics, monitors, and instruments, and so changeovers between acts stay fast and organized.
fields.practical_application: A stage tech runs the stage patch, dresses and tapes down cable, resets mics and backline between acts, and fixes onstage problems like a dead mic or fallen stand during the show, taking direction from the monitor engineer or stage manager.
common_mistakes: Thinking the stage tech mixes sound; they set up and support the stage while the monitor and front-of-house engineers do the mixing.
Neglecting cable management, leaving trip hazards and unmarked lines that slow changeovers and troubleshooting.
UNSAFE: Running mains or audio cable across walkways without taping, ramping, or matting it, creating trip-and-fall hazards on a dark stage.
UNSAFE: Lifting or moving heavy backline and cabinets alone instead of using team lifts or dollies, risking back and musculoskeletal injury.
scenario_contexts: Setting the stage patch and placing mics before a festival changeover.
Dressing and taping down cable runs across the stage before doors.
Quickly replacing a failed vocal mic mid-set at the monitor engineer's call.
